core: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total quantity of real output (real GDP) that all buyers in an economy want to purchase at each aggregate price level
AD sums the four spending components: consumption (C), investment (I), government purchases (G), and net exports (X - M)
The AD curve is drawn with the aggregate price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis
The AD curve slopes downward because of three macroeconomic channels: the wealth (real-balances) effect, the interest-rate effect, and the exchange-rate (net-export) effect
These three reasons are different from why a single good's demand curve slopes down (substitution and the income effect on one good's relative price)
A change in the price level is a MOVEMENT along AD; a change in a determinant (confidence, fiscal policy, monetary policy, foreign income, exchange rates) SHIFTS the whole AD curve
Rising consumer or business confidence, expansionary fiscal policy, expansionary monetary policy, higher foreign income, and a weaker domestic currency shift AD right; the opposites shift it left
supporting: Consumption is the largest single component of U.S. aggregate demand (illustrative BEA figure ~67% of GDP in 2020)
AD meets aggregate supply to set the equilibrium price level and real GDP (one-sentence hand-off to the aggregate-supply topic)
outOfScope: The aggregate supply (AS) curve and its slope/shifts (owned by economics:foundations:aggregate-supply)
The full AD-AS equilibrium analysis beyond one sentence (aggregate-supply)
Deriving the C + I + G + NX component definitions in detail (owned by economics:foundations:gdp; cited here, not re-derived)
The mechanics of the fiscal-policy and monetary-policy tools themselves (owned by economics:foundations:fiscal-policy and :monetary-policy; named here as shifters)

claims.claim: Aggregate demand is the total amount of spending on domestic goods and services in an economy, and the aggregate demand curve shows the total quantity of real output (real GDP) buyers want to purchase at each aggregate price level.
Aggregate demand is composed of consumption (C), investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports, exports minus imports (X - M).
The AD curve is plotted with the aggregate price level (GDP deflator) on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis.

The wealth (real-balances) effect: a higher price level erodes the buying power of savings held in money and fixed-value assets, reducing wealth and therefore consumption spending, so quantity of real output demanded falls as the price level rises.

The interest-rate effect: a higher price level makes the same purchases require more money and credit, pushing interest rates up, which reduces business borrowing for investment and household borrowing for homes and cars, lowering I and C.

The exchange-rate / foreign-price (net-export) effect: if U.S. prices rise while foreign prices stay fixed, U.S. goods become relatively more expensive, so exports fall and imports rise, reducing net exports and the quantity of real output demanded.

The reasons the AD curve slopes downward differ from the reasons a single good's demand curve slopes downward; for a single good the decline is driven mainly by substitution toward other goods, whereas the aggregate price level cannot be escaped by substituting to 'other goods in general.'

Rising consumer confidence raises consumption and rising business confidence raises investment, shifting AD to the right; falling confidence shifts AD to the left, and pessimistic public statements can act as a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Expansionary fiscal policy (higher government spending or tax cuts) shifts AD right and contractionary fiscal policy (lower spending or tax increases) shifts AD left; the Federal Reserve shifts AD through interest rates, with lower rates stimulating consumption and investment and higher rates discouraging borrowing.

Aggregate demand and aggregate supply reflect competing macroeconomic perspectives (Keynes' law, demand creates its own supply; Say's law, supply creates its own demand), and a full picture requires both sides; AD meets AS to determine the equilibrium price level and real GDP.
Consumption is the largest single component of U.S. aggregate demand, illustratively about 67% of GDP in 2020.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether stabilizing aggregate demand through active fiscal and monetary policy is effective or desirable.
positions: Keynesian view: inadequate aggregate demand explains short-run recessions and unemployment, so demand-side policy can stabilize output.
Classical / Say's-law-leaning view: supply drives output, especially in the long run, and demand-management policy is less effective or can misfire.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as competing schools, per the subject's positive-vs-normative control. The lesson teaches the positive mechanics of AD (definition, slope, shifters) and only names the policy debate; it does not declare a winner. Policy tools are handed off to the fiscal-policy and monetary-policy topics.

unsupportedExistingClaims: No machine-generated draft for this topic exists in the published lessons.json (economics is a later-phase subject not yet merged), so there was no prior boilerplate to correct.
correctionsNeeded: Guarded the classic confusion between a MOVEMENT along AD (caused by a price-level change) and a SHIFT of AD (caused by a determinant change).
Made explicit that the AD downward slope comes from the wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects, NOT from the substitution/income logic that explains a single good's demand.
Labeled the fiscal/monetary stabilization debate as contested and named the school-of-thought split rather than implying consensus.
Dated and attributed the single illustrative consumption-share figure to BEA.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, Section 11.2: Building a Model of Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the AD definition (total spending on domestic goods and services), the four components C + I + G + (X - M), the axes (price level vertical, real GDP horizontal), and the three reasons the AD curve slopes downward: the wealth effect (a higher price level erodes the buying power of savings, cutting consumption), the interest-rate effect (higher price level raises money/credit demand and interest rates, cutting investment and durable-goods borrowing), and the foreign price / exchange-rate effect (a higher domestic price level makes exports relatively expensive, cutting net exports). Also supports that these macro reasons differ from a single good's demand slope. NC-SA license: reference-only, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, Section 11.4: Shifts in Aggregate Demand
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the determinants that shift AD: consumer confidence (raises consumption), business confidence (raises investment), fiscal policy (higher spending or tax cuts shift AD right; lower spending or tax increases shift it left), and monetary policy (lower interest rates stimulate consumption and investment; higher rates discourage borrowing), plus the note that interest rates affect exchange rates and thus net exports, and that pessimistic statements can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. NC-SA license: reference-only.
